title: JTAG-Accessible Memory BIST on the AMD AUP ZU3
summary: Modern chips contain hundreds or thousands of embedded memories, and memories take a large share of the chip area. Because memory cells are the densest structures on silicon, they are where manufacturing defects most often appear. Every memory must therefore be tested after production, and often again in the field. Chips include **MBIST**: on-chip hardware that applies test algorithms to the memories, compares the results and reports pass/fail and the failing locations.
tools: AMD AUP ZU3 board (Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC), Vivado (Simulator, IP Packager, IP Integrator), Vitis
prerequisites: Digital logic and FSMs, an HDL (Verilog/SystemVerilog), C programming
goals: **Specify the system:** memories under test, fault types, March algorithms, controller instruction format, TAP instructions, the IEEE 1687 network (SIBs and TDRs) and the clock modes.

**Design the test IPs** in SystemVerilog and package each as a Vivado IP: TAP controller, SIB and TDR cells, programmable BIST controller, collars, fault-injection wrappers, clock/mode controller, functional traffic generator.

**Support at least five algorithms** (MATS+, March X, March C$-$, March SS, checkerboard) as microcode programs, the **eleven fault types** of “Fault models”, and **three modes**: functional, BIST-slow, BIST-at-speed.
**Cross clock domains safely** between TCK, the BIST clock and the functional clock, and prove it in simulation and with Vivado's CDC report.

**Verify each IP** with its own self-checking testbench, and the complete system end to end through the JTAG pins with a class-based, constrained-random environment, reference models, assertions and functional coverage.
**Run the fault-coverage experiment** on the board over JTAG: at least 50 random faults per fault type, every algorithm, all memories, slow and at-speed. Compare the results with the theory.
**Implement the system** on the AUP ZU3 with the at-speed clock meeting timing (target 250 MHz).
outcomes: explain memory fault models and why March tests detect them;
explain and implement the IEEE 1149.1 TAP and an IEEE 1687 network;
design a programmable controller (instruction format, sequencer) in SystemVerilog;
design clock-domain crossings and glitch-free clock switching on an FPGA;
package designs as reusable IP and assemble them in IP Integrator;
build a layered, class-based SystemVerilog testbench with reference models, SVA and functional coverage;
plan and analyse an experiment, and present the results as tables and plots.
